sm: Dallas Jenkins, creator and director of The Chosen, is interviewed about the series. It is the first gospel-focused TV retelling of Christ's story and holds a Guinness record as the most translated show, now in over 130 languages. Jenkins says that after a big movie flopped he adopted what he calls the five and two plan, the name of his company, Five and Two Studios: his job is only to provide the loaves and fish, and God decides the results. He says the show is an artistic portrayal, not scripture, and that everything in it is meant to be plausible and true to the character and intentions of Jesus. To keep himself accountable he has a council of Bible experts who read scripts, and he is contractually bound to adjust them if they raise a red flag, which has happened only two or three times.

Jenkins says he is the one person responsible for the words on screen, with no outside influence beyond his inner circle. He does not require the cast and crew to share his faith, and says people of many backgrounds or none are united around doing great work, and most have stayed for all seven seasons. He tries to love and lead them well each day. Asked about keeping urgency, he says season one was made by artists with no audience, while season seven had nearly ten times the resources and hundreds of millions of viewers, yet the set still treats the work as sacred and aims for excellence over pleasing people. He says the crucifixion and resurrection seasons got the same commitment as the first, since every word of Jesus mattered. Recalling his 2017 film failure, he compares it to the feeding of the five thousand, where Jesus brought the crowd to hunger so that only a miracle could answer it, and says the show's success reminds him he is not good enough to have built this himself.

Jenkins describes walking in his front yard on the last day of filming, telling God to look at what he has done, and says his reliance on the Lord has only grown. Asked about theaters, he says releasing episodes there was a first for a TV show, and others have since followed. He says people form friendships at screenings, and it can be easier to invite someone to a theater than to church. The season six finale was filmed as a feature film for a global theatrical release in over twenty-five languages. Season six, the crucifixion season, premieres November 15 on Prime Video with the first three episodes, then one per week, and covers twenty-four hours ending with Jesus's death. Its key theme is following the path he chose, since Jesus willingly went forward from Gethsemane and could have stopped it. Jenkins says the season still includes joy, beauty and some humor, because the crucifixion is the greatest act of love.
